content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore xml-to-json and json-to-xml conversion within XML Generation, Serialization, and Conversion. You will connect its syllabus topics to an inspectable example, check the expected result, and note tool/version limits.
content.why_it_matters: XML-to-JSON and JSON-to-XML Conversion matters because XML workflows rely on explicit structure and predictable processing. The lesson helps you reason about differences between data models, avoid a common misunderstanding, and make a result reproducible for another developer.

content_blocks.caption: The visual introduces xml-to-json and json-to-xml conversion; inspect the worked example and then verify it.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Generation and conversion must preserve data semantics, escaping, character encoding, and namespace identity. XML and JSON do not share identical data models, so conversion rules must explicitly handle arrays, attributes, mixed content, and repeated elements.

content_blocks.title: Connect the subtopics
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly covers: Differences between data models; Representing arrays and repeated elements; Attribute representation; Mixed-content limitations; Designing predictable conversion rules. Treat these as connected parts of one workflow: define the structure, make the relevant assumptions explicit, and verify a result with a small known input.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: XML-to-JSON and JSON-to-XML Conversion
content_blocks.expected_output: A JSON object expresses product records as an array. Define explicit conversion rules for attributes, mixed content, namespaces, and repeated XML elements.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this example as text. Run it only in a processor that supports the shown language/version; the standard CodeLeaf playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only and does not execute XML, XSD, XPath, XSLT, XQuery, Python, or SQL. Prefer XML-aware builders and serializers over string concatenation. Test round trips with empty, repeated, multilingual, namespaced, and special-character values; a syntactically valid output can still lose information.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the sample to its exact starting state before each experiment. Change one element, attribute, expression, or constraint at a time, then compare the result with the expected behavior.
content_blocks.limitations: This snippet is an inspectable example, not an XML execution service. Validate it with a standards-compatible XML processor; feature support depends on the processor/version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Distinguish well-formedness, schema validity, and application-level correctness; they are different checks.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small synthetic example that demonstrates “Differences between data models”. Then add one boundary case involving “Representing arrays and repeated elements”. Write down what should happen before testing, and record the exact output or processor message afterward.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a document is correct because it looks readable.
common_mistakes.why: Visual appearance does not prove well-formedness, schema validity, correct namespace handling, or application-level meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse and validate the document with the intended processor, then assert its meaning using a focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing specification features with processor support.
common_mistakes.why: A standard may define features that a specific runtime does not implement.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the version and feature support; test with the actual target processor.

common_mistakes.why: Missing values, wrong types, namespace differences, or boundary inputs can expose failures.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a valid case, an invalid case, and an edge case to the verification notes.
